t: Minimum Time to Complete All Deliveries — Binary Search + Hall's Condition
o: Drone i is unavailable at hours that are multiples of rᵢ. For a horizon T, drone i alone has fᵢ = T − ⌊T/rᵢ⌋ free hours. Deliveries must be assigned to distinct hours with each drone using only its free hours. By Hall's theorem over the two drones, a schedule exists iff d₁ ≤ f₁, d₂ ≤ f₂, and d₁+d₂ ≤ |A₁∪A₂| = T − ⌊T/lcm(r₁,r₂)⌋ (an hour is unusable by both only when it is a multiple of the lcm). Verifying example 2 at T=6: union = 6−3 = 3 < 4, infeasible; T=7 gives 4 ≥ 4. Feasibility is monotone in T, so binary search the answer.
k: Feasibility for two drones is exactly Hall's condition: individual capacities plus the union bound T − ⌊T/lcm⌋.
Free-capacity counts fᵢ = T − ⌊T/rᵢ⌋ are monotone, enabling binary search on T.

a.n: Approach 1: Incremental Scan with Feasibility Check
a.i: Try T = 1, 2, 3, … and return the first T passing the three Hall conditions. Conceptually simplest; fine when the answer is small.
s: Define ok(T): f1 ≥ d1, f2 ≥ d2, and T − T//L ≥ d1 + d2.
Increment T until ok(T) holds and return it.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on the Horizon (Optimal)
a.i: Since ok(T) is monotone (each term T − ⌊T/c⌋ is non-decreasing), binary search the smallest feasible T between 1 and 2·(d₁+d₂)+L, which is always feasible because each free count is then at least half of T.
s: Binary search with the ok predicate.

w: The key trap is assuming f₁+f₂ total capacity suffices — shared free hours get double-counted (example 2 proves it); the union bound via lcm fixes this. Use 64-bit intermediates since dᵢ can be 1e9. Follow-up: generalize to m drones (Hall over all 2^m subsets) or ask for the actual hour assignment.
